Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. Networks (TCNs) have shown great promise for handling time-series data. However, optimizing the time-dilated convolution aspect of TCNs requires a considerable amount of experimentation. We've developed an automatic optimizer that tackles this challenge by treating dilation factor optimization as a weight pruning problem on the time-axis. This method learns dilation factors alongside model weights during a single training process, leading to significant reductions in model size and inference latency on real hardware by up to 7.4x and 3x respectively, without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, it enables the discovery of multiple Pareto-optimal TCN models from a single starting point, outperforming manually designed solutions in both model size and accuracy.

Tononzintla 2 shows a typical pattern of alpha-element enrichment, similar to other high-metallicity globular clusters. massive arc-like structure, dubbed a Giant Arc, which lies at a redshift of approximately 0.8. Spanning nearly 1 billion light-years, this feature exhibits remarkable symmetry when viewed from space. It was discovered through a novel approach using intervening magnesium-absorbing systems in the light from background quasars. Our analysis leverages a range of techniques: hierarchical clustering, a statistical test, and power spectrum analysis - each method providing unique insights, which together suggest the presence of a massive structure at around 4.5 standard deviations from expectations. We employed multiple statistical tests to mitigate any biases that could influence our findings, which suggest that the arc-like feature is an overdensity with a density ratio of about 1.3, with a 4.4-standard-deviation confidence level. The Giant Arc raises intriguing implications for the distribution of massive structures throughout the universe and may shed new light on the cosmological model. It is crucial to further explore this feature using future high-resolution spectroscopy, allowing us to study the Giant Arc in greater detail and analyze any exotic particles that may be present.

using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has gained significant attention. Two primary approaches, direct methods and two-stage pipelines, can be distinguished based on whether intermediate cues are employed. In the latter category, CNNs first regress intermediate cues such as 3D object coordinates or virtual control points in the initial stage. These intermediate cues then facilitate the computation of object pose through constructed correspondence constraints. This paper focuses on refining two-stage pipelines by integrating two distinct concepts: projection grouping and correspondence learning. We begin by utilizing a local patch-based method to generate projection heatmaps, representing the confidence distribution of projected 3D bounding box corners. A projection grouping module is then introduced to eliminate redundant local maxima from heatmaps. In contrast to directly applying the perspective-n-point (PnP) algorithm, multiple correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and their neighborhoods, and ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Ultimately, the proposed framework selects correspondences with higher confidence to determine object pose, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods in extensive experiments on three public datasets.

Bond-Based Peridynamics, despite some limitations, has become a widely used tool in numerical simulations due to its ease of implementation and intuitive understanding. This paper reviews and examines multiple aspects of bond-based peridynamic models. A comprehensive overview of peridynamics theory, its applications, and numerical models is provided, including a detailed examination of employed integral kernels and their differences. The implications of their mathematical structure are discussed, including the role of nonlocality, kernel structure, material impenetrability, and the influence of PD kernel nonlinearity on crack formation prediction. A critical analysis of these aspects is presented, followed by a proposal to extend BB-PD to fluids within the framework of fading memory materials, offering insights into the deeper understanding of peridynamics in fluid dynamics.

This library builds upon the Graphical Lasso method, initially introduced in (Friedman 2007), which estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$. Originally proposed by (Dempster 1972) under the name Covariance Selection, the framework has been expanded to include latent variables in (Chandrasekaran 2012) and more recently to jointly estimate multiple inverse covariance matrices, as seen in (Danaher 2013; Tomasi 2018). The GGLasso package supports the solution of a general formulation, encompassing significant special cases, including the single Graphical Lasso with latent variables, the Group, and the Fused Graphical Lasso.

By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, the authors' previous work on sampling accuracy has been expanded upon, allowing for the identification of stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. For harmonic oscillators, certain schemes yield exact configurational averaging results, potentially leading to improved performance in biomolecular modeling, where bond stretches play a significant role. In general systems, an optimal method can be identified that exhibits very low bias in comparison to other alternatives. The results of simulations on the alanine dipeptide (both solvated and unsolvated) show that higher accuracy is achieved without compromising computational efficiency, allowing for large timesteps and maintaining the conformational exploration rate. The optimal scheme proves to be a superior algorithm for molecular sampling, offering efficiency improvements of 25% or more in practical timestep sizes in vacuum and reductions in configurational average errors by a factor of ten or more in solvated simulations at large timesteps.

In our research, we've been investigating how dark matter behaves around equal-mass black hole binaries, discovering a stable, long-lasting profile that emerges and grows over several orbits. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the potential universal symmetries present within the spectrum of charged black holes. By analyzing the outcomes of conformal field theories in an AdS framework and black hole physics, we investigated whether the presence of charged black holes eliminates universal symmetries. Our findings indicate that the presence of charged black holes does indeed preclude certain universal symmetries. Nonetheless, we discovered that a wider class of universal symmetries may still be present, encompassing those that appear in holographic descriptions of conformal field theories. Hence, we propose that the spectrum of charged black holes possesses a form of "holographic universal symmetry," which we believe is a fundamental characteristic of all quantum gravity theories.

  Our objective is to minimize the number and intricacy of hardware and software components that a mobile user must trust to withstand malicious inputs. We propose a multi-domain hardware design consisting of isolated, statically-partitioned trust domains. To enable a program to temporarily access both processing and input/output functions exclusively and simultaneously, we introduce simple, formally-verified hardware components. For managing this hardware, we present OctopOS, an operating system comprising mutually distrustful subsystems.
  We have implemented a prototype of this system, combining hardware and OS on a CPU-FPGA board, and demonstrate that it incurs a minimal hardware cost compared to contemporary system-on-chip designs. For security-sensitive applications, this system significantly reduces the necessary trust compared to conventional trusted execution environments while achieving reasonable performance. For regular applications, performance is comparable to legacy systems.

Our adversary model assumes a sophisticated opponent who can manipulate the reward and transition at any step within an episode, but only up to a certain percentage of episodes. Our model is more aggressive than previous approaches. We initially demonstrated that no algorithm can find a significantly better policy than one that is slightly suboptimal, given our attack model. Notably, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can maintain robustness if the reward corruption is limited, and can find a near-optimal policy. To address unbounded reward corruption, we developed the Filtered Policy Gradient algorithm, which can find a nearly optimal policy despite significant corruption. multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun.

lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Next, we applied a dimerization to the hopping terms and observed the migration of the Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along curved trajectories. Additionally, we outline the potential realization of this model using CO atoms on top of a Cu(111) surface.

yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated through a process called quantum-optical catalysis. This process utilizes a beam splitter (BS) or parametric amplifier (PA) to produce these states. SPCCSs are produced when a coherent state and a single-photon Fock state are input into a BS or PA, and a single photon is detected in one of the output channels. The probabilities of successful detection differ depending on whether BS or PA catalysis is used. It has been proven that SPCCSs generated by BS and PA devices are identical, as evidenced by their photon number distributions. Further analysis has revealed the non-Gaussian nature of SPCCSs, which exhibit sub-Poissionian distribution, anti-bunching, quadrature squeezing, and a negative Wigner function. These findings demonstrate the nonclassical properties of SPCCSs, which can be leveraged for various quantum technological applications.

CT scans can be very difficult due to low contrast, varying anatomy, and the presence of foreign objects. To overcome this, doctors often rely on additional information from endoscopic findings, medical history, and other imaging tests, which can be time-consuming and produce inconsistent results. This study investigates whether it's possible to automate the process of segmenting esophageal tumors from CT scans alone. To achieve this, we developed a fully automatic method based on convolutional neural networks, called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), which focuses on the most relevant features and regions. We tested this method on a large dataset of 792 scans from 288 patients with varying anatomies and conditions, and the results showed a high degree of accuracy with a simplified clinical workflow. Our code is available for public use.

This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering.

However, existing research on nested NER typically applies a linear structure to model nested entities, despite their inherent hierarchical nature. To address this limitation, this study models nested entities as a unified structure and proposes a novel parsing algorithm to identify all entities simultaneously. Moreover, to leverage the benefits of corpus-level information, this work introduces a new set of features based on Point-wise Mutual Information and corpus-aware statistics. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our holistic modeling approach, which achieves promising results on standard benchmarks and outperforms state-of-the-art models in some cases. We test our methods using a particular problem related to a type of curve called a plane quartic, and we look at how the geometry of this curve changes when we view it in different ways. We express the reasons why certain curves and their intersections may not behave well in terms of how their shapes change when viewed in different ways. We also show how to calculate the importance of certain curves and their intersections in terms of their shapes and the way they are defined. This allows us to confirm a prediction made by other mathematicians about the importance of certain types of curves and their intersections in certain types of fields. Our results rely on a theorem that helps us understand how the geometry of fields changes when we view them in different ways.

This study examines the current state of natural language processing research, highlighting its limitations and potential drawbacks in addressing five critical areas for the greater good: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, misinformation, and hate speech in multilingual communities. Microwave Background (CMB) could serve as evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model, which proposes the universe undergoes cycles of expansion and contraction. These patterns include low-variance circles resulting from black hole mergers and Hawking points resulting from black hole evaporation. A high-resolution search of the Planck and WMAP CMB data using machine learning software found that previous evidence for low-variance circles was likely due to CMB anomalies. Removing these anomalies revealed no statistically significant low-variance circles. Similarly, no statistically significant Hawking points were found when accounting for CMB anomalies and using a Gaussian temperature amplitude model. However, the absence of distinct Hawking point features does not disprove the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model, as a large density of Hawking points could create an interference pattern in the CMB. To further investigate this possibility, the Hawking point density is estimated throughout the CMB, yielding a statistically significant result of 0.24 quanta per steradian with an error of 0.07 quanta per steradian. If the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model holds, the merging of black hole rings should contribute to a statistically significant multipole bias in the CMB, which was found to be 0.34 delta steradians with an error of 0.15 delta steradians. This research provides new insights into the nature of the CMB and its relationship to the Conformal Cyclic Cosm

Our primary objective is to elucidate how the widespread use of embeddings in NLP is influenced by the term distribution within a given corpus. We utilize a mathematical framework to highlight the implicit assumptions regarding language structure inherent in this model. Our analysis reveals that Markovian assumptions provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are formed and how they capture frequentist synonyms. These assumptions enable the creation of generative models and an explicit analysis of the commonly used loss function in NLP. Infective to Recovered (SIR) epidemic model on a social network is conducted. The underlying social network is modelled as an Erdos-Renyi random graph but, during an outbreak, individuals connected to infected neighbours may sever or re-establish connections. As the population grows, the model converges, revealing both the early branching process-like behaviour and the main phase of the epidemic process, which is equivalent to a deterministic model and a pair approximation model. The total number of individuals infected during a major outbreak is also studied, yielding a law of large numbers. Two key findings emerge: (i) the limiting fraction of infected individuals may exhibit a discontinuous jump from 0 to a positive value at the critical infection rate and (ii) when rewiring is restricted to uninfected individuals, the limiting fraction of infected individuals jumps from 0 to 1 at the critical infection rate.

Our measurements yielded a significantly smaller gap size of approximately 5.5 meV, establishing a new superconducting gap structure around the zone corner and resolving prominent controversies

To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. The model was then used to analyze the impact of acoustic vibrations on the jet flame, which showed that a reduction in equivalence ratio leads to a decrease in reaction rates, while an increase in turbulence reduces reaction rates due to the formation of secondary Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings.

These clusters exhibit distinct and complex dynamics when compared to repulsively-bound pairs in gases with no inter-site interactions. Unlike on-site pairs, nearest-neighbor dimers in these models undergo an interactive quantum walk, resulting in a unique dynamics with multiple time scales. The methods described in this report enable the simulation of observable quantities related to CRE caused by ultra-high energy photons, such as densities, energy spectra, and particle orientation at the top of the Earth's atmosphere.

groups of objects have diverse uses and are frequently represented graphically as a 2-tier layout, where each group is displayed as a set of nodes on separate horizontal lines, and the relationships between them are depicted by lines connecting corresponding nodes on the two lines. One common aim in these visualizations is to minimize the number of intersecting lines, but another goal is to maximize the overall space efficiency of the visualization, especially when the number of connections exceeds the number of items in each group. To address this challenge, we define a new measure of space efficiency in these visualizations, called the area complexity, and investigate the general binary classification problem of determining whether a given bipartite graph layout can be optimized to achieve a specific target area complexity. Our analysis reveals that this problem is NP-hard to solve directly, but we can efficiently solve it for a specific subclass of bipartite graphs, and we also develop an algorithm that can identify a optimal solution in a much smaller subclass. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the class of polynomial-time solvable instances is a proper subset of the class of efficient instances, and we develop a tool that can be used to identify the class of efficient instances more accurately. Our analysis also yields a new insight into the relationship between the size of the graph and the minimum area complexity that can be achieved, and we prove that a specific property is equivalent to the optimal solution being achievable with a target area complexity in a later time period.

Nonetheless, there are still several open issues, including the ability to process continuous visual data and the management of class imbalance in datasets. Current research tackles these problems separately, whereas they often coexist in real-world applications. In this study, we focus on the challenge of learning from incrementally imbalanced datasets, where the complexity of the deep model remains constant and the memory is limited to storing exemplars of past classes across incremental stages. Since the memory is restricted, older classes are learned from fewer images than new classes, exacerbating the initial class imbalance. Consequently, a bias towards new classes emerges, and we assess a range of score calibration methods to mitigate it. We conduct our evaluation using three datasets, two imbalance configurations, and three bounded memory sizes. The results demonstrate that most calibration methods yield beneficial effects, particularly in scenarios with lower bounded memory sizes, which are more relevant to practical applications. As a secondary contribution, we investigate the effect of removing the distillation component from the loss function of incremental learning algorithms and find that vanilla fine-tuning serves as a more robust foundation for imbalanced incremental learning methods.

In addition to this new technique, the study identifies the underlying causes of performance degradation through cache eviction and uncovers a previously unknown source of slowdown. explain the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, we employed an Effective Field Theory (EFT) approach. Although the Standard Model (SM) contribution of the Higgs to the muon's magnetic dipole moment is minimal, a bottom-up EFT analysis reveals that the Higgs could still resolve the anomaly if its interactions with other SM particles deviate from their predicted values. Applying unitarity principles, we found that such a solution would imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of around 10-18 TeV, which could be lowered to 5 TeV if the Higgs interactions with the W and Z bosons conform to SM expectations. This scenario could also result in a notable increase in the muon's electric dipole moment, making it accessible to future sensitivity limits. To explore this possibility in more detail, we used the Caswell-Lowdon expansion in the EFT language, identifying the most significant parameter as the product of two Higgs boson moments with the muon's momentum. We then analyzed the constraints on this parameter from various experiments, including LHC Run 2 and future colliders such as CEPC, FCC-ee, and CLIC. Our study indicates that a solution to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment could remain elusive, with New Physics residing beyond the reach of near-future experiments and requiring further investigation in future Higgs and muon physics studies.

study, we concentrate on vertical federated learning (VFL), which allows multiple entities to jointly train a robust machine learning model using shared features, without exchanging sensitive information. Based on collaboration patterns, VFL can be distinguished from horizontal federated learning. Our focus is on identifying potential privacy breaches in real-world VFL systems. To achieve this, we have developed and implemented two real-world privacy attacks: a reverse multiplication attack targeting the logistic regression VFL protocol, and a reverse sum attack targeting the XGBoost VFL protocol. Our empirical results demonstrate that the attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and easy to execute, even when intermediate outputs are encrypted. The leaked information can be used to train a new classifier that performs as well as the original model. We also explore potential countermeasures and their challenges, with the goal of opening up promising research avenues. This research aims to raise awareness about the privacy risks in VFL and initiate further study in designing privacy-preserving VFL protocols.

Tetralogy of Fallot patients primarily depends on heart chamber volume and function, according to current guidelines. These biomarkers can be accurately measured by analyzing three-dimensional images obtained from cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) scans. Recent studies have shown that U-Net architectures have achieved impressive results on provided data in several grand challenges. However, clinical data sets are often more diverse and complex, reflecting individual pathologies and scanner properties. Moreover, there is a scarcity of specific training data for rare diseases such as Tetralogy of Fallot. This work investigates two aspects: the accuracy gap when training models on one data set and applying them to another, and the feasibility of achieving similar results with a more heterogeneous data set. Multiple deep learning models were trained and evaluated using four-fold cross-validation, demonstrating that models can achieve excellent results within a single data collection. Pyramid Networks (FPNs), have been facing a long-standing challenge. Researchers have observed that the performance of FPN-based detectors tends to decline for large-scale objects. This paper re-examines FPN's role in the detection framework, attributing its success to optimization perspectives. It also identifies the root cause of the decreased performance as the emergence of improper back-propagation paths after integrating FPN, which restricts each backbone network branch to focus on specific scale ranges. To address this issue, two strategies are proposed to enable each backbone network branch to consider all objects within the FPN-based frameworks. Firstly, auxiliary objective functions are introduced to facilitate direct back-propagation signals for various-scale objects during training. Secondly, a more rational feature pyramid construction method is proposed to eliminate irrational back-propagation paths. Experimental results on the COCO benchmark validate the analysis and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, achieving significant improvements (over 2%) in various detection frameworks, including one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors.

This paper focuses on a specific type of conditional model that defines the distribution of variables $X$ and $Y$ in relation to $X$. Traditional methods of evaluating network attacks focus on macro-level metrics, including the critical probability of network fragmentation and the size of the largest remaining component, without examining the attack from a micro-level perspective, such as the removal of individual nodes and their effects. This paper presents and applies a novel approach focusing on the micro-scale of network attacks. Based on percolation theory, we analyze the phenomenon of avalanches triggered by the removal of a single node from the network, where the removal of a node within the giant component causes other nodes to disconnect from it, significantly contributing to network fragmentation. Specifically, we focus on the parameter of avalanche size, which represents the number of nodes disconnected from the giant component due to a single node removal. For a random attack on a Cayley tree network, we derive an analytical distribution of avalanche sizes throughout the entire attack, until the network is dismantled and the attack is terminated.

Given an irreducible simple algebraic group G and a Borel subgroup B, consider an irreducible subgroup P containing B, and let P' be its derived group. A theorem by Richardson states that the algebra of P semi-invariants is multiplicity-free. A linear subvariety e+V that induces an isomorphism between the algebra of P semi-invariants and the algebra of e+V is called a Weierstrass section. In this work, a Weierstrass section is constructed in type A, with a focus on its application rather than its construction. The nilfibre relative to the action of P is denoted by N, and it is shown that a point e in N can be used to describe the structure of a unique irreducible component C of N. The description of e+V provides an explicit characterization of C as a B saturation set, which is a subalgebra of the Lie algebra of the nilradical of B. However, this subalgebra may not be complemented, and therefore, C may not be an orbital variety closure. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that C can be empty, and this is shown to occur in a specific example in A10.

Research has been conducted on over-parameterized linear models in conjunction with high-dimensional data that is not necessarily sparse; yet, existing findings rely on the independent sampling assumption. This study investigates a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where samples are dependent. An estimator is proposed via interpolation, accompanied by a theoretical framework for assessing excess risk under multiple types of dependence. This framework enables the treatment of infinite-dimensional data without the need for sparsity and handles long-memory processes uniformly. Furthermore, the risk in our theory is bounded using the integrated covariance and non-degeneracy of autocorrelation matrices. The results demonstrate that the convergence rate of risks for short-memory processes is equivalent to that of independent data, whereas long-memory processes impede convergence. Additionally, several examples of specific dependent processes are presented, applicable to our framework.

To address the class-imbalance issue, we propose a novel AL algorithm called Balanced Selection (BASE), which selects more balanced samples for annotation than existing methods, resulting in consistent outperformance of random sampling. However, the formulation of DP in graph contexts is complex due to interconnected data points, hindering individual privacy loss calculation in differentially private learning. This work introduces a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method, based on the positive-P phase-space formalism, to model interacting Bose gases. This method surpasses existing approaches in its ability to simulate the full quantum behavior of these systems, including non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. Typically, the formation of PTMs following edge localized modes (ELM) is attributed to magnetic field ergodisation and the emergence of a seed magnetic island. This study, however, proposes an alternative explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A notable feature of plasma turbulence is the presence of coherent, long-lived structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. These localized, magnetic-field-aligned regions exhibit varying plasma densities and carry parallel currents. By interpreting ELM filaments as massive blobs and the interspace between them as holes, the study demonstrates that a closed current filament can produce magnetic fluctuations similar to those measured by the JET in-vessel magnetic pickup coils when a PTM is present. This suggests that capturing a hole on a q=3 surface after an ELM crash can generate a PTM equivalent signature, while capturing the ELM filament itself on a q=4 surface can produce an outer mode signature.

This method fosters a cooperative behavior among robots, ensuring they avoid each other reciprocally. The repulsive field, influenced by a robot's velocity and position relative to others, is activated when a robot is on a collision course with other mobile robots or stationary obstacles. The annealed large deviation principle for the empirical process of words involves a rate function that is the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words relative to the reference distribution of words. In a previous study, the quenched large deviation principle, which is conditional on a typical letter sequence, was derived for renewal times with an algebraic tail. This resulted in a rate function consisting of two terms, one being the annealed rate function and the other proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by concatenating words and randomizing the origin. The proportionality constant was the tail exponent of the renewal process. This paper aims to extend both large deviation principles to non-i.i.d. letter sequences by demonstrating that they carry over when the sequence satisfies a mixing condition called summable variation. The rate functions are again specific relative entropies relative to the reference distribution of words or letters, but several approximation arguments are necessary to achieve this extension due to the non-i.i.d. nature of these reference laws.

a surge of interest in the intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) technology. This technology utilizes passive reflective elements capable of adjusting the phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization of incoming waveforms. Given its unique properties, the characteristics of wireless channels can be manipulated to optimize signal design and processing for specific applications, such as radar systems, where it has the potential to significantly enhance performance. This paper provides a theoretical framework for integrating IRS technology into radar systems, with a focus on improving target parameter estimation. We explore the potential of IRS in scenarios where the line-of-sight link is weak or obstructed and demonstrate its ability to create a virtual, non-line-of-sight link between the radar and target, leading to improved radar performance. Numerical simulations reveal that the IRS-enhanced virtual link can effectively estimate moving target parameters, even in non-optimized scenarios, as long as the non-line-of-sight link is relatively stronger than the line-of-sight link by a factor of around 10^-1.

In software testing, mutation analysis is the benchmark for evaluating test quality by assessing the ability of a test to detect artificial faults; if a set of tests fails to detect such mutations, it will also fail to detect actual bugs. However, the traditional mutation analysis method is impractical for fuzzing due to its high cost, as it requires independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper applies innovative mutation analysis techniques that group multiple mutations together, allowing for the first time to evaluate and compare fuzzers using mutation analysis. An evaluation framework for fuzzers is introduced and applied to several popular fuzzers and test subjects. The results demonstrate how this approach enables assessing fuzzer performance and measuring the impact of enhanced techniques. Although current fuzzers can only identify a small percentage of mutations, this outcome presents a challenge for future research, particularly in improving (1) detecting failures beyond general crashes and (2) triggering mutations and faults.

They demonstrated that these games allow for the existence of $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific conditions for $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$. Nevertheless, they left unanswered the question of how difficult it is to identify such an equilibrium. Our work presents a query-efficient reduction from broader classes of games to $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, which we leverage to establish a query lower bound for any randomized algorithm seeking to find $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player, binary-action, $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, with the bound being exponential in $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. -fold cross-validation, a process that involves randomly dividing data, leading to stochastic estimates with considerable variability, particularly in natural language processing tasks. This variability undermines the reliability of parameter tuning, as the selected parameters are highly susceptible to the partitioning method used. Consequently, optimal parameters are frequently overlooked, and reproducibility is severely compromised. To address this issue, we introduce the concept of J-k-fold cross-validation, which involves conducting J independent k-fold cross-validations to evaluate model performance. Our contributions extend this method from performance estimation to parameter tuning, and we investigate the optimal selection of J and K. We contend that minimizing variability is more crucial than minimizing bias for effective parameter tuning, and therefore recommend lower values of K, allocating the saved computational resources to increase J. To validate our suggestions, we conduct an in-depth examination of various case studies, including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging, and document classification.

Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple knowledge-learning objectives with efficient, lightweight student networks. of dense suspensions undergo a sudden and dramatic transformation in their flow behavior, characterized by an abrupt thickening. This phenomenon is believed to be a precursor to a rigidity transition, triggered by a shift in the dominant interactions between suspended particles from hydrodynamic to frictional forces. Our research provides a comprehensive theory of viscosity, describing its behavior as a universal function that bridges the frictionless jamming point to a rigidity transition influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Experimental evidence from two distinct systems - cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol - demonstrates that viscosity can be condensed into a single, universal curve spanning a broad range of stresses and volume fractions. The resulting collapse reveals two distinct scaling regimes, each with unique critical exponents, indicating that frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming belong to separate universality classes. By incorporating material-specific behavior into a scaling variable that gauges proximity to shear jamming, our reformulation enables the application of established theoretical frameworks for equilibrium critical phenomena to elucidate fundamental physical aspects of the shear thickening transition.

This reaction is characterized by a sudden increase in the transverse electric field that peaks at a specific point and then drops. This peak amplitude remains consistent across various types of superconductors despite their differences, which poses an interesting phenomenon to investigate further. This peak is essentially a representation of the minimum viscosity-to-entropy ratio in the vortex liquid, which in terms of units $\frac{\hbar}{k_B}$, is much greater than what is observed in common liquids. Moreover, there's a distinction to be made between the entropy held within the vortex core and the entropy bound to a moving magnetic flux line. A crucial aspect to consider here is that the entropy within the vortex core undergoes a continuous exchange with the surrounding normal quasi-particles due to a normal steady flow, which causes a decrease in the entropy bound within the core as the vortex moves at a slower speed. A vortex will eventually release all the entropy bound within its core within a specific distance, which is on the order of the coherence length of the superconducting material. This will occur provided that the ratio between the energy gap and the Fermi energy is sufficiently large.

ysics is the common envelope phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped by the outer layer of one of them. The interactions between the stars and the surrounding layer cause the orbit to contract. This phase can ultimately lead to the merging of the stars or a subsequent series of interactions. Mergers involving compact objects, such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes, can produce a range of spectacular astrophysical events, including supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and gravitational waves. Due to the diversity of initial conditions and the complexity of the processes involved, predicting the final state of common envelope phases is challenging. In large-scale calculations, such as population synthesis models, conservation laws are often employed. This study develops a novel approach to utilizing angular momentum to derive a simplified formula for the final orbital separation in common envelope phases, offering advantages in the study of binary and multiple star systems, particularly in the context of potential mergers. This work primarily focuses on common envelope phases in binary star systems, while a companion paper extends the methodology to more complex multiple star systems.

By expanding the Einstein equations in terms of transverse gradients, our numerical results match exact solutions at the first order of expansion. The Einstein equations can be broken down into two sets of differential equations, where one set contributes negligibly to boundary observables. This simplifies the computation to solving planar shockwave equations and a few additional differential equations for each 'pixel' in the transverse plane. This results in a significant speedup of roughly one order of magnitude for numerical solutions at the first order of expansion, with errors of less than 10% at the hydrodynamization time and for low to mid rapidities.

we've analyzed the large-scale structure of ionized and molecular gas in the starbursting galaxy IRAS08339+6517, located 500 parsecs in size. Our study has uncovered a direct relationship between the mass flux of star formation-driven gas outflows and the galaxy's star formation rate. The data suggest that outflows are closely linked to the galaxy's ability to recycle gas, with areas of high star formation rates expelling more gas than they consume through star formation. These findings support the idea that outflows play a crucial role in regulating the galaxy's ability to sustain short gas depletion times. Our results highlight the importance of further studies on gas outflows in galaxies to better understand their role in galaxy evolution.

However, the complexity of building probabilistic models has limited its widespread adoption. To address this, we introduce BoAnon, a SBO framework that learns system structure from logs. BoAnon offers an API for experts to incorporate system knowledge as performance models or component dependencies. By combining the learned structure with expert-provided knowledge, BoAnon creates a probabilistic graph model that enables the optimizer to discover efficient configurations more quickly than other methods. In a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a significant improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. BoAnon's innovative approach to contextual structure learning makes SBO more accessible for a variety of computer systems, including databases and stream processors.

As alternative non-parametric approaches often sacrifice efficiency, this paper introduces a robust parameter estimation technique for discretely observed data from parametric stochastic process models, leveraging the advantageous properties of the density power divergence measure within the framework of minimum distance inference. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing structure-preserving discretization techniques, which involve proving standard methods' preservation of certain properties and proposing innovative schemes that achieve high accuracy while preserving key properties of the original equation. However, when combined with implicit time-stepping methods, these schemes have a significant drawback: their preservation properties typically rely on the exact solution of the systems of equations defining each time-step, which becomes impractical for large linear systems resulting from typical space-time PDE discretizations. This paper proposes an adjustment to the flexible generalised minimum residual (FGMRES) iteration that incorporates selected constraints on approximate numerical solutions, and demonstrates its application to both conservation laws and dissipative systems.

We have derived flexible criteria that can not only verify ergodicity across most known sequence combinations, but also enable resolution for some outstanding issues. Our research focuses on the early stages of superbubble evolution, including pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae. We aimed to investigate the growth of dust grains within orbiting dusty clumps and the superbubble's swept-up supershell, as well as the survival of dust grains produced by sequential supernovae. Our model takes into account the gravitational potential of the star cluster and the self-gravity of the parent cloud, as well as radiative cooling and a state-of-the-art population synthesis model for the coeval cluster. Our findings show that in massive molecular clouds hosting a super star cluster, dust grain growth increases the dust mass at a rate of approximately 4.8 times 10 to the negative 5 solar masses per year during the first 2.5 million years. Furthermore, pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae contribute significantly to the superbubble's dust budget, resulting in the creation of massive amounts of dust without relying on a top-down process. This process is consistent with the large dust mass observed in galaxies during the early stages of cosmic reionization.

or far-field 3D detection, is a crucial challenge for autonomous vehicles operating at high speeds. To ensure safe braking distances, accurate detection of far-field obstacles is essential. However, existing benchmarks, such as the nuScenes dataset, do not adequately address this problem as they only evaluate performance up to a certain distance. This is partly due to the difficulty in obtaining far-field 3D annotations, particularly from lidar sensors that often produce few point returns for distant objects. Moreover, current 3D detection metrics employ a one-size-fits-all approach, which is inconsistent with the varying tolerances required for human vision and stereo disparities. As a result, the Far3Det task is not thoroughly analyzed. For instance, the conventional wisdom that high-resolution RGB sensors are vital for detecting far-away objects is contradicted by the current benchmark leaderboards, which show lidar-based methods ranking higher. To address this, we developed a method to create a well-annotated far-field validation set from the nuScenes dataset and proposed a Far3Det evaluation protocol. We also explored various 3D detection methods for Far3Det and demonstrated that high-resolution RGB sensors significantly improve detection in the far-field. Furthermore, we introduced a simple yet effective fusion method that combines detections from RGB and lidar detectors, which outperforms state-of-the-art 3D detectors in the far-field.

the potential energy surface (PES) of molecules, which represents their energy levels in relation to their nuclear positions. Nevertheless, calculating this data is a complex task due to the need to sample a vast number of ground states across the PES, especially when considering that only a small portion of the dataset is typically involved in the reaction process. This research introduces a novel approach, called ReEvolved, which employs a two-step evolution process to sample the PES. The first step involves a global evolution scheme, such as the neural network-based ML3 - a massive learning algorithm, that maps the nuclear coordinates to the ground state wavefunction. The second step involves a local optimization of the wavefunction to converge to the nearest ground state for a given nuclear configuration. ReEvolved is unique in that it combines two distinct transformations: a contraction of the electron density to a more compact form, which makes the calculation more efficient, and a rotation of the electron density to account for correlation effects. This research employs a development version of the FDFNT algorithm as the global evolution scheme. To assess the performance of ReEvolved, it was applied to three benchmark cases, including hydrogen chains and diamond-based molecules, and compared to other algorithms. The results show that ReEvolved can accurately predict the bond length and dissociation energy with good agreement to experimental and theoretical data from other studies. Additionally, ReEvolved demonstrates superior performance in terms of efficiency, requiring less computational resources and achieving faster convergence compared to other algorithms

This is a complex task due to the sparsity and noise in intraoperative data, real-time constraints, and unknown variables such as tissue properties and boundary conditions. The liver's lack of distinct surface features and the different types of noise in imaging modalities make correspondence establishment extremely challenging. We train a convolutional neural network to simultaneously search for surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network is trained on biomechanical simulations of randomly generated, deforming organ-like structures, enabling it to generalize to new patient organs without retraining. We introduce noise into intraoperative surfaces during training to make the network robust to noisy data. The network outputs a displacement field during inference, aligning the preoperative volume with the partial intraoperative surface. Our experiments demonstrate the network's ability to translate to real data while maintaining high inference speed. The accompanying code is publicly available online.

Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge.

This concept, initially explored in the 1970s, combines properties of matchings, Hamiltonian cycles, and edge colourings. This study focuses on cubic graphs and aims to identify those where every perfect matching corresponds to a colour in a proper 3-edge-colouring. This is equivalent to determining whether such graphs are even-2-factorable, meaning all their 2-factors consist solely of even cycles. Since bipartite cubic graphs are trivially even-2-factorable, we concentrate on non-bipartite cubic graphs. A cubic graph with the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property is a sufficient but not necessary condition for being even-2-factorable. This work introduces a family of even-2-factorable non-bipartite cubic graphs, known as papillon graphs, and examines the parameters for which these graphs possess the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property or are simply even-2-factorable. Additionally, we prove that a papillon graph with a specific parameter set is a snark, a type of cubic graph, and demos a snark's first known instance with the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property.

Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields.

By selectively pumping a nonlinear resonator with a coherent field, we induce a chiral interaction between the resonators, allowing us to create an all-optical diode and a three-port circulator. This chiral coupling enables our device to work with both single-photon pulses and strong light, offering an isolation ratio of over 40 dB and fidelity of more than 98%. Moreover, we've demonstrated the ability to switch nonreciprocal transmission on and off with a relatively weak pump light, effectively creating an all-optical three-port valve. We also show that our approach can be extended to design nonreciprocal quantum optical devices.

The DED2D system also allows D2D communications to share the same spectrum as the base station. However, D2D interference and wireless link propagation loss can significantly degrade the data throughput of information-demanded users. While generated responses are often evaluated for their semantic and syntactic quality, the encoder's internal representation is frequently overlooked. Since this representation is crucial for predicting relevant responses, evaluating the encoder's performance is a significant yet complex challenge. In this research, we demonstrate that relying solely on human or automated metrics to assess the quality of generated text is insufficient for truly evaluating a dialogue model's understanding of language. To address this limitation, we propose a set of probe tasks to assess the encoder's representation in various dialogue models. Our experiments reveal that certain probe tasks are more easily learned by sophisticated models, while others prove more difficult. Interestingly, our findings suggest that RNN-based architectures outperform transformer models on these probe tasks, despite underperforming on automated text generation metrics. This indicates that RNNs might be better suited for preserving task-specific information compared to transformers.

However, extracting robust and efficient 3D LiDAR descriptors that remain invariant to changing conditions and orientation remains a challenge. To address this issue, a novel deep learning network called AttDLNet is proposed, which leverages a range-based proxy representation and an attention mechanism to selectively focus on long-range context and inter-feature relationships. The network is trained and validated on the KITTI dataset, and results show that the addition of attention improves performance, enabling more efficient loop closures and outperforming existing LiDAR-based place recognition approaches. The ablation study indicates that the middle encoder layers are most effective, while deeper layers are more resistant to orientation changes. The AttDLNet code is publicly available on GitHub.

-On-Demand or live, demands adapting video streams to match viewer devices' specifications, which involves transcoding and incurs significant computational costs. As video streaming demands surge, Streaming Service Providers are increasingly relying on cloud services to ensure Quality of Service, leveraging heterogeneous Virtual Machines with varying prices from cloud providers. To optimize cloud utilization for video transcoding, it's essential to thoroughly analyze transcoding performance on different cloud VMs. This research provides the first comprehensive analysis of video stream transcoding on heterogeneous cloud VMs, enabling accurate predictions of transcoding time and informed scheduling methods. Based on this analysis and considering cost differences, a model is proposed to assess the suitability of each cloud VM type for specific transcoding tasks, providing resource provisioning methods with balanced performance and cost trade-offs for efficient cloud utilization in video streaming.

As a result, they struggle to generate high-quality paragraph-level speech that demands expressiveness and naturalness. To address this, a context-aware speech synthesis system called MaskedSpeech is proposed, which incorporates both contextual semantic and acoustic features. MaskedSpeech draws inspiration from speech editing techniques, masking current sentence acoustic features and combining them with contextual speech, then using the result as additional input. The phoneme encoder learns contextual text information from neighboring sentences, and cross-utterance semantic features are used to enhance prosody generation. MaskedSpeech is trained to reconstruct masked acoustic features using contextual information, and experimental results show that it outperforms the baseline system in terms of naturalness and expressiveness.

We introduce a new ensemble approach that surpasses existing contextualized methods, which we use to investigate the predicted semantic changes in English words across a 50-year period. Our analysis reveals that contextualized methods often mistakenly flag words with significant change scores, even when they are not experiencing genuine semantic evolution. We delve into specific cases and propose a classification system for these challenging instances. Our findings indicate that pre-trained contextualized language models are prone to conflating changes in word meanings and contextual fluctuations, inherent to their distributional nature, as well as merging semantic and syntactic aspects of words. This involves using the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear relationship between four key variables: radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements and other factors, we determine the minimum spin rates of a group of heavy, jetted AGNs. These results allow us to investigate the implications for ultra-light particles, specifically scalar, vector, and tensor types, in the mass range of $10^{-20}$ to $10^{-19}$ eV. In this study, we utilized long-term, high-speed imaging techniques to visualize zebrafish retinas in real-time during early development, aiming to uncover the underlying mechanisms governing nuclear behavior during this process. Our high-resolution images enabled us to accurately track the movement and division of numerous tightly packed nuclei, which were then used to develop and test a theoretical model of retinal IKNM as a diffusive process driven by a concentration gradient of nuclei at the upper layer. Practical code patterns in these applications are characterized by being non-negative, systematically structured, and often deviating from the incoherence properties of patterns like Gaussian codes, which can negatively impact reconstruction performance. This paper contributes to the design of code patterns for video compressed sensing and demosaicing by minimizing the mutual coherence of the matrix $\boldsymbol{\Phi \Psi}$, where $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ is the sensing matrix derived from the code, and $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$ is the signal representation matrix. The key innovation of this work lies in explicitly incorporating the unique structural properties of code patterns required by these applications: (1) non-negativity, (2) block-diagonal structure, and (3) circular shifting, particularly the latter enabling accurate and seamless patch-wise reconstruction in certain compressed sensing architectures.

By breaking down the abundance patterns into two distinct components, we were able to identify the signatures of core collapse supernovae and Type Ia supernovae in the stars. The analysis revealed a complex picture, with various elements showing different behaviors. Elements created by core collapse supernovae, such as magnesium and silicon, tend to be more abundant in stars formed from heavy molecular clouds, while those created by Type Ia supernovae, like nitrogen and oxygen, are more abundant in stars formed from light molecular clouds. This study of star abundances provides a comprehensive picture of the elemental creation and destruction processes in the galaxy, offering insights into the many complex factors that shape the abundance patterns of the stars.

Consequently, there is an urgent need to understand and control the spread of online rumors. To address this, we examined the dynamic process of rumor spreading based on the exchange between the public and the media. The initial spread of rumors was influenced by the population's trust in information and the diversity of news sources. This was initially discovered by analyzing the noise kernels associated with the stress-energy tensor of quantum fields. In this study, we revisit this phenomenon using a quantum thermodynamics approach, examining the heat capacity and quantum compressibility of model spacetimes filled with a quantum field at both high and low temperatures. The heat capacity, in particular, is a measure of energy density fluctuations, and a ratio exceeding unity raises questions about the validity of the canonical distribution. Similarly, a system's compressibility is a criterion for the validity of the grand canonical ensemble. We derive the free energy density and calculate the heat capacity and compressibility for various spacetime geometries, including 2D Casimir space, 2D Einstein cylinder, and 4D Einstein universe, as well as higher-dimensional Einstein universes. This comprehensive analysis enables us to investigate the thermodynamic stability of quantum matter fields and make observations about the compatibility conditions for the coexistence of quantum fields and spacetimes, a fundamental issue in the intersection of quantum mechanics and gravity.

Focusing on the deep-inelastic scattering regime, we establish the corresponding moment sum rules for the structural functions. These moments are determined by the thermal expectation value of twist-two operators, which can be computed using first principles in lattice QCD for the initial moments. Furthermore, we demonstrate how lattice QCD calculations can be employed to investigate the minimum photon virtuality required for the Bjorken scaling of structural functions to become applicable. Additionally, we provide a parton-model interpretation of the structural functions in the Bjorken limit and validate its consistency. In this context, the kinematic variable $x$ is directly related to the longitudinal momentum carried by the partons, and its range extends from zero to infinity. By choosing a parton momentum parametrization of the form $x T u$, where $u$ represents the fluid four-velocity and $T$ its temperature in the rest frame, the parton distribution function for a plasma of non-interacting quarks is found to be proportional to $x \log(1+e^{-x/2T})$.

unclonable encryption, a technique that prevents an adversary from creating multiple ciphertexts decrypting to the same original message. This notion is revisited, and the following advancements are presented:

  - Enhanced Security: Previous constructions either offered one-time security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. New constructions provide unclonable encryption schemes with semantic security, meeting minimal cryptographic requirements for both public-key and private-key settings.
  - Improved Lower Bound and Generalized Construction: The information-theoretic one-time secure construction by Broadbent and Lord was analyzed, revealing a success probability of $0.85^n$. A generalized construction based on a broader class of monogamy of entanglement games is proposed, along with cloning attacks achieving probabilities of $0.71^n$ and $0.75^n$ against specific schemes.
  - Implications for Copy-Protection: Unclonable encryption satisfying a stronger property, unclonable-indistinguishability, implies copy-protection for a specific class of unlearnable functions. Although current encryption schemes do not meet this criterion, this connection offers a new path to construct copy-protection mechanisms.

The analysis involves a model comprising an encoder, decoder, and adversary, with the latter having access to the message, a non-causal noisy representation of the transmission, and unlimited transmission capabilities. The presence of lattice relaxation in the sample causes the flat band to blend with remote valence bands, leading to significant differences in the contribution of interband transitions to the plasmon dispersion and energy. Under conditions where only intraband transitions within the doped flat band are considered, low-damped and quasi-flat plasmons arise. Conversely, a $\sqrt q$ plasmon dispersion is observed when interband transitions between the flat band and remote bands are also taken into account. The plasmon energies can be adjusted through twist angles and doping levels. However, in rigid samples without lattice relaxation, both lower-energy quasi-flat plasmons and higher-energy interband plasmons can coexist. For highly doped rigid samples, enhanced interband transitions can suppress the quasi-flat plasmons. Our study highlights the importance of two key factors, the isolated flat band and a suitable hole-doping level, for observing the low-damped and quasi-flat plasmon mode in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides. The findings of this research may provide valuable insights for studying strong plasmon-mediated coupling in these systems in the future.

Lowering PET radiotracer doses or scanning times reduces photon counts, potentially compromising image quality. Recent advancements in deep learning allow for the transformation of low-quality PET images, acquired with significantly lower doses, into high-quality images by incorporating associated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. This uncertainty-aware framework, suDNN, uses multimodal inputs, including low-dose PET images and multi-contrast MRI data, to generate high-quality PET images, thereby enhancing its robustness to novel acquisitions. Experimental results on in vivo PET-MRI data and various forms of out-of-distribution data demonstrate the superiority of suDNN over current state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through the SETI initiative, with a key focus on identifying Dyson Spheres - massive energy-gathering structures surrounding stars that support advanced civilizations. This study examines the feasibility of constructing a Dyson Sphere around a black hole, considering six potential energy sources, including the cosmic microwave background and relativistic jets. It is estimated that a Dyson Sphere would require at least $4\times10^{26}\,{\rm W}$ to support a Type II civilization. Our analysis indicates that an accretion disk would be the most effective energy source, with a luminosity of $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$, and that collecting additional energy types could increase the total energy by approximately fivefold. Furthermore, our results suggest that a Dyson Sphere surrounding a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way would be detectable via waste heat radiation in various wavelengths, making it potentially identifiable using current telescopes such as the Galaxy Evolution Explorer.

A method to achieve this involves using active measurement tools that inject artificial traffic and assess network performance through probes. However, these tools consume a lot of resources and can only cover a small portion of what could be measured, which can lead to missing SLA breaches. The definition of this limited scope is currently handled by human administrators, who lack the scalability and adaptability needed for dynamic networks. This article explores the potential benefits of using peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to enhance the detection of SLA breaches. Secondly, we present measurement session activation strategies based on these principles, which do not require human intervention, are adaptable to network condition changes, and independent of the underlying active measurement technology.

, cutting-edge long-baseline neutrino experiments heavily rely on accurate models of neutrino interactions with atomic nuclei. These models contribute significantly to the overall systematic uncertainty due to the limited ability of existing detectors to detect final state neutrons. Next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments will incorporate three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers in their near detectors, which boast superior timing resolution and fine granularity. This technology enables the measurement of neutron kinetic energy in neutrino-argon interactions on a per-event basis, thus providing valuable data to refine neutrino interaction models and improve neutrino energy reconstruction. Prototypes of these detectors have been tested at the neutron beamline at Los Alamos National Laboratory, exposing them to neutron energies between 0 and 800 MeV in 2019 and 2020. To validate their neutron detection capabilities, the total neutron-scintillator cross section was measured and compared to external data, yielding a value of 0.36 $\pm$ 0.05 barn between 98 and 688 MeV.

In this study, we investigated how the presence of surface water impacts these particles. Typically, laboratory conditions involve multiple water layers on the grains, but in the low-pressure environment of protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only have a single water layer. As dust moves inward, even this layer eventually evaporates in higher temperature zones. To account for this, we re-examined the tensile strength of the same chondritic material we previously studied under normal laboratory conditions, but this time using two new preparation methods: drying the dust in air (dry samples) and heating it in a vacuum (super-dry samples). For temperatures up to 1000 K, our data for dry samples showed that their sticking forces increased by approximately ten times compared to wet samples. Up to 900 K, super-dry samples behaved similarly to dry samples. However, their sticking forces then increased exponentially to another factor of approximately 100 at about 1200 K. The increase in sticking from wet to dry samples follows a trend observed in amorphous silicates and extends to multimineral mixtures. The findings for super-dry dust suggest that aggregate growth is enhanced in a small, high-temperature region around 1200 K, which could be a favorable environment for planetesimal formation.

Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we investigated the superconducting properties of a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with Rashba spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman magnetic field. Our findings indicate that Rashba spin-orbit coupling has a positive impact on s-wave superconductivity. When superconductivity is suppressed by the Zeeman field due to Pauli pair-breaking, the Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field by mixing the spins, thus restoring superconductivity at finite temperatures. This favorable effect of the spin-orbit coupling arises from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the amplitude for the propagation of a pair of electrons in time-reversed states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for sufficiently large Rashba coupling and Zeeman field, the superconducting state is expected to exhibit a topologically non-trivial nature by examining the Fermi surface of the interacting model.

We propose that this complex rift history plays a primary role in shaping the conjugate passive margin systems.

The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. A formal framework for a new algebra, called the bootstrap algebra, has been established through a direct, explicit calculation. A connection between the bootstrap algebra and the Heisenberg algebra has been made via a classical limit approach. A major finding is that the anomalous NG theorem can only be violated at a threshold where the symmetry breaking parameters transcend from a continuous global Lie group structure to a discrete Lie algebra structure, marked by the emergence of a quasi-Heisenberg algebra, which can be identified through the formation of bootstrap algebras, characterized by an exact, explicit calculation, involving a mixture of Lie algebra and number theory, focusing on the Heisenberg algebra, whose calculation is absent in the current literature, possibly due to the algebra's non-Lie nature.

graphene holds significant promise for creating materials with large lattice mismatches, fabricating freestanding membranes, and reusing expensive substrates. Nevertheless, conclusive experimental evidence for a remote epitaxial process remains scarce. Many instances of exfoliatable single-crystalline films can be attributed to contaminants at the graphene/substrate interface, prompting alternative explanations such as pinhole-seeded lateral epitaxy or van der Waals epitaxy. We discovered that the large lattice mismatch between hexagonal boron nitride and graphene is mitigated by the formation of domains with a 30-degree rotation on Khaledia substrates. This observation can be accurately described by a combination of two smaller epitaxial domains, suggesting that one of the graphene domains is coated with a BN layer during the growth process. Furthermore, our research reveals that the efficiency of this process scales with the size of the epitaxial domain, indicating that larger domains have a lower energy. Our findings provide experimental support for a remote epitaxial process, particularly one that utilizes the epitaxial constraints of the substrate to minimize lattice mismatch.

GeV radiation remains a mystery, and researchers suggest that hadronic emission from magnetic arrest disks around black holes could be the solution. According to this theory, particles in the disk are accelerated through magnetic reconnection and turbulence. By applying this model to the 15 brightest radio galaxies, we found that it can explain GeV radiation if the rate at which material falls towards the black hole is very low. However, at higher rates, the gamma-rays are absorbed by interactions with low-energy photons. If we consider another theory for how electrons are heated by magnetic reconnection, the model fails to match the data for most galaxies, highlighting the importance of electron heating rates. Additionally, applying the model to the Galactic center revealed that gamma-rays there are not produced by the disk around Sgr A*. We estimated the cosmic ray intensity from Sgr A* but found it too low to account for the high-energy cosmic rays detected on Earth.
